item.text:
**I would deprioritise terfenadine itself as a lead, but keep the chemistry as a reference point.** ToxPred flags hERG blockade (0.68 against its 0.41 classification threshold), but that score does not measure block potency or clinical risk. The decisive evidence is already clinical: when CYP3A4 inhibition caused unmetabolised terfenadine to accumulate, QT prolongation occurred in healthy volunteers. Terfenadine was subsequently withdrawn in the US because its benefits no longer justified that risk once fexofenadine was available. [Clinical interaction study](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/article-abstract/404621); [FDA history](https://www.fda.gov/about-fda/fda-history-exhibits/drug-therapeutics-regulation-us).

Fexofenadine, terfenadine’s active acid metabolite, shows why the series may still be useful: experimental work found hERG block with terfenadine but no block with fexofenadine at the concentrations tested. That is a useful direction for analogue design, though each new compound needs its own exposure and safety assessment. [Electrophysiology study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1573545/).

I would run the next work as a short, paired series:

1. **Measure concentration-dependent hERG current block** for new analogues, with terfenadine and fexofenadine as controls. Relate potency to projected *unbound* human exposure, including a plausible high-exposure case.
2. **Measure H₁ potency and pharmacokinetics together.** Quantify parent and metabolites, identify CYP3A4 dependence and likely inhibitor interactions, and check whether the structural changes that reduce hERG block preserve H₁ activity.
3. **Test the non-sedating premise** with brain penetration or central H₁ occupancy evidence for promising analogues. For compounds that clear the early gates, assess cardiac risk with the broader ion-channel and QT work appropriate to an integrated programme. [ICH E14/S7B guidance](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/e14-and-s7b-clinical-and-nonclinical-evaluation-qtqtc-interval-prolongation-and-proarrhythmic).

I would treat ToxPred’s three positive Tox21 calls as follow-up flags, not established toxicities. Its applicability check covers element composition only; it does not establish structural similarity to its training data.
